cue: Adding up spending on final goods and services.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>GDP</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{GDP}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mi>C</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>G</mi><mo>+</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>−</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= C + I + G + (X - M)</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Imports are subtracted; transfers and used goods are left out.

cue: Comparing the cost of the same basket across years.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>CPI</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{CPI}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>basket cost now</mtext><mtext>basket cost in the base year</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{basket cost now}}{\text{basket cost in the base year}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: The base year is always 100; divide by the base year, not the other way round.

front: The inflation rate: the percent change in a price index.
cue: From two years of CPI or the GDP deflator.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>inflation rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{inflation rate}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mtext>new index</mtext><mo>−</mo><mtext>old index</mtext></mrow><mtext>old index</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{new index} - \text{old index}}{\text{old index}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Divide by the old index; a fall in inflation (disinflation) is not deflation.

cue: Turning nominal GDP into real GDP, or the reverse.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>GDP deflator</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{GDP deflator}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>nominal GDP</mtext><mtext>real GDP</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{nominal GDP}}{\text{real GDP}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Real GDP = nominal / deflator x 100: students often multiply instead.

front: A real value (real GDP, a real wage).
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>real value</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{real value}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>nominal value</mtext><mtext>price index</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{nominal value}}{\text{price index}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Use the index of the same year as the nominal value.

cue: From counts of employed and unemployed people.
trap: The labor force is employed plus unemployed, not the whole adult population.

cue: How much of the adult population works or looks for work.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>participation rate</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{participation rate}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mtext>labor force</mtext><mtext>adult population</mtext></mfrac><mo>×</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{\text{labor force}}{\text{adult population}} \times 100</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Discouraged workers leave the labor force: the unemployment rate falls though no one found a job.
Cyclical unemployment is not in it; cyclical = actual minus natural.

cue: How much real GDP changes per dollar of new spending.
trap: MPC + MPS = 1; with MPC 0.8 the multiplier is 5, not 1.25.

front: The tax multiplier (negative: a tax rise lowers output).
cue: The effect of a change in taxes or transfers.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>tax multiplier</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{tax multiplier}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mtext>MPC</mtext></mrow><mtext>MPS</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{-\text{MPC}}{\text{MPS}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Its size is always one less than the spending multiplier.

front: The change in spending that closes a gap.
cue: A recessionary or inflationary gap and an MPC.
trap: Divide, do not multiply; decide the direction first.

cue: How far new excess reserves can expand the money supply.
formula: <math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mtext>money multiplier</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{money multiplier}</annotation></semantics></math><wbr><math class="mac-m"><semantics><mrow><mo form="infix">=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mtext>required reserve ratio</mtext></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">= \frac{1}{\text{required reserve ratio}}</annotation></semantics></math>
trap: Multiply excess reserves, not total deposits; a cash deposit does not change the money supply at first.

front: The real interest rate: the nominal rate minus expected inflation.
cue: Lenders, borrowers and the loanable funds market.
trap: Unexpected inflation lowers the real rate a lender earns.

front: Excess reserves: what a bank may lend.

cue: Money growth and inflation in the long run.
trap: With V and Y steady, faster money growth shows up as inflation.
